To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

AMPAR‐mediat ed Ca2+ transients in the axons of cerebell ar molecular layer interneurons are amplified by Ca 2+ ‐ induced Ca 2+ release from internal stores, and that these events contribute to GABA release from the terminals of these cells.
Ca2+ permeable AMPARs located in the axons of cerebellum molecular layer interneurons are responsible for the induction of Ca2+ transients and the release of neurotransmitter in the axon terminal.
Ca2+ permeable AMPARs located in the axonal varicosity of cerebellar MLIs are activated by glutamate released from PFs and that the resulting [Ca2+] signal triggers GABA release.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the functional role of Ca2+ entry through Ca2+‐permable AMPARs in the axonal varicosity of MLI.
the mechanisms of glutamatergic transmission at the cerebellar parallel fibres–Mol layer interneurone synapses.
the mechanisms underlying synaptic plasticity and the role of AMPA receptors in this process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Ca‐permeable, GluR2‐lacking AMPARs in axonal boutons of MLIs can be activated by spillover glutamate and that these receptors contribute to the modulation of GABA release.
Ca2+ influx through AMPARs in MLI axons may be an additional mechanism for GABA release in cerebellum.
the axon terminals of MLI express GluR1, 2, 3 and 4 AMPAR subunits, which are Ca2+ permeable.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Ca2+ permeable AMPA receptor (Ca2+‐pAMPAR) are located in the axon terminals of cerebellar interneuron and are activated by glutamate spill over from parallel fibres (Ca2+ spillover).
Ca2+ influx through AMPARs in MLI axonal varicosites is a mechanism to enhance GABA release by Ca2+ signalling.
Ca2+ influx through Ca2+‐ permeable AMPARs can be an important mechanism for regulating synaptic transmission in cerebellar MLIs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
AMPARs can act as Ca2+ channels in axon terminals.
Ca2+ influx through Ca2+‐ permeable AMPARs in axonal terminals is sufficient to induce Ca2+‐dependent exocytosis.
AMPA receptors in axon varicosities can be activated by spillover glutamate and trigger Ca2+-dependent exocytosis of synaptic vesicles.
